title: Live from New Delhi: What the World's Financial Leaders Fear Most
description_html:
What does the global economy look like from the rooms where some of the world’s biggest investment and business decisions are made? Stephanie Flanders is in New Delhi for Bloomberg’s New Economy Forum, where she speaks with Bloomberg Chief Economist Tom Orlik about the risks building beneath the surface — from higher borrowing costs to the vast sums flowing into artificial intelligence.

Then, in a session hosted by Bloomberg New Economy Editorial Director Erik Schatzker, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, Blackstone President Jon Gray and Tata Sons Chairman N. Chandrasekaran debate what really matters in this new era of uncertainty — and which trends they believe are powerful enough to bet on anyway.

cues.t: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
Podcasts.
Radio.
News. I think the biggest thing, when we look back in history, when we look back 10, 20 years from now, will be the technology.
Because I think that's the thing that's going to define this era.

That we're moving from a place like we did in the U.S. from 1870 to 1900 with the Industrial Revolution, that when you bring this superintelligence to the entire world that it's going to profoundly change how we live, how consumers live, how businesses are impacted, and how governments oversee societies.
And to me, that's the big thing.
I'm Stephanie Vlanders, head of government and economics at Bloomberg, and this is Trumponomics, the podcast that looks at everything in the economic world of Donald Trump.
And this week, I'm in India, where Bloomberg is holding its annual New Economy Forum for the first time in New Delhi.
There have been a slew of luminaries here from the world of business and finance, along with many government ministers from around the world.
I counted at least a dozen.
I'm recording this on Wednesday, which is day two, after a very grand opening session yesterday featuring a barnstorming speech from the Prime Minister, Narendra Modi.
I'm not going to play that to you because, frankly, I don't think it would come across.

But we did have the President and Chief Operating Officer of Blackstone, the world's biggest private equity investor, and the Chairman of Tata & Sons, India's biggest multinational, in the opening panel session, along with the former UK Prime Minister, Rishi Sunak.
Now, I know panels aren't always exciting, but this one, I thought, really told you how the world looked right now to people at that level.
And as you'll hear, it's not necessarily the way it looks to you and me, or indeed people in the White House.
That's in a minute.
But first, I also wanted to give you a taste of another section of that first morning.
In fact, a few minutes after Prime Minister Modi spoke, we had a presentation from our very own Global Chief Economist, Tom Orlick, who you've heard regularly on this podcast.
And he decided to go back to that summer hit, Christopher Nolan's film of The Odyssey, to enliven his presentation around the global economy.
Tom, thank you very much for being here.
Great to be here, Stephanie.
Now, I was thinking back, Elon Musk, I seem to remember, accused Christopher Nolan of trashing Homer's grave.
That film.
was a woke.
Cry of pain for the end of the rule-based global order, which obviously Elon Musk didn't like.
Ezra Klein, the columnist for the New York Times, thought that was precisely why it was, in his words, the political movie of the decade.
Everybody found something in that film.
Tom, you saw lessons for economic policy in it.

I'm sure classics scholars would tell me that this is off-base, Stephanie, but it seems to me that one of the themes that comes through in The Odyssey is this idea of a world where the rules of hospitality have broken down.
You see it in Polyphemus the Cyclops, a host who eats his guests.
You see it in Penelope's suitors, guests in Odysseus's house, eating his food, drinking his wine, trying to steal his wife.
I thought this idea of the Odyssey and a world where the rules of hospitality have broken down will be a kind of neat framing for a presentation to the audience.
So what are some of the consequences from an economic standpoint of this world where the rules of hospitality are broken down?
So I think one of the places where we're seeing this dynamic play out is in the US bond market.
If we think about the cost of borrowing for the US Treasury, back in 1980, that was around 15%.
Over many decades, the cost of borrowing for the US Treasury fell and fell until by 2020, it was close to zero.
Now, in the last few years, that trajectory has changed, and the cost of borrowing for the US isn't falling anymore.
It's rising. The 10-year rate is now north of 5%.
And I think that's a reflection of some of these big dynamics that we're seeing.
A world where war is more likely, and so companies have to borrow more to pay for defense.
A world where there's been rupture between the US and China, the US and Russia, the US and the petrostates.
So these countries, which in the past were willing to put their savings to work in the US treasury market, are now not doing that anymore.
And a world where geopolitical shocks like the Iran war are pushing inflation higher.
And of course, bond investors need to be compensated for higher inflation.
So in this world where the rules of hospitality have broken down, the US Treasury has to pay more to borrow.
And of course, when the US Treasury has to pay more to borrow, everybody has to pay more to borrow.
A fact which is pretty consequential for our hosts here in India, hoping to attract more FDI to finance the build-out of their infrastructure and their manufacturing base.

One of the other themes that came through, which obviously has been much discussed in this conference, is AI is actually something that might surprise some people, that we have seen with the build-out of AI, in many ways, a kind of reassertion of global supply chains, at least in a certain part of the economy, and reanimation of globalisation and trade.
And with that... the return of very large global imbalances.
So despite Donald Trump's best efforts, China exporting more than it ever has.
We actually had new record trade surplus numbers coming out of China this week.
And the US, despite Donald Trump's efforts, importing, we reckon, $500 billion more a year than in 2016.

That's allowing for inflation, not all from China, but it has in many ways become more dependent on the rest of the world as a result of, in part, AI and other things about the way the world has gone.
But as you pointed out, the flip side of that is big trade surplus and surplus revenues for China, Korea, Taiwan are We've seen those before.
They used to be invested via central banks into US treasuries often.
What's different this time?
It's strange.
President Trump imposed these sweeping tariffs to try and reduce the US trade deficit, reduce the Chinese trade surplus.
In fact, what we've seen in the last couple of years is actually those surpluses and deficits have exploded higher, right?
We've now got surpluses in China, Taiwan, Korea, and deficits in the US that are bigger in dollar terms than they were back in the early 2000s before the global financial crisis.
But as you note, Stephanie, there's also a different dynamic at work.
In the early 2000s, let's take China as an example, the trade surplus meant a huge pileup of dollar savings in the economy.
Those dollar savings were managed by the People's Bank of China Central Bank, a very conservative buy and hold investor.
And the PBOC put those dollars into the US Treasury market, the most stable, safest asset in the world.
This time around, the savings piling up in East Asian countries, they're not being managed by central banks.
They're being managed by private investors, much more nimble, much more focused on returns, And when we look at the data, what we see is they're not going into the treasury market anymore.
That's one of the reasons the treasury is having to pay more to borrow.
They're going into stocks.
They're going into corporate bonds.
The pretty clear signal is that they're going into the AI revolution, right?

So you've got this circular flow of funds where the US is importing a huge amount of chips to build out its data centers and And the countries making those chips are taking the dollars the US is paying them and turning around and investing them back in the US AI companies.
Now, if you're an AI optimist, and there's lots of reasons to be an AI optimist, that's all good, right?
AI is going to make us better off.
This is accelerating the AI revolution, which is going to make us all better off.
But if you're an AI pessimist, And you think the profits from AI might turn up a day late and a dollar short.
And there's going to be a moment where there's a big adjustment in the markets, a crash.
This dynamic means the pain from that crash is going to be spread out around the world.
It does certainly sound like a risky combination.

What was striking to me was A slightly different view from that panel I mentioned at the start, although they, at least one of them, was pretty focused on the risks lurking in government debt and government balance sheet.
So let's hear from that now.
And I'm actually going to let my colleague, Eric Schatzker, the editorial director of NEF, who presided over the panel, do the introduction.
Distinguished guests, I'd like to say a few things about our panelists to explain why we've invited them to join me here on stage this morning.
Rishi Sunak, as you know, is a sitting member of parliament in the UK and, of course, the country's former prime minister.
He has become a strategic voice in Silicon Valley as an advisor and also as a visiting fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution.
He has also rejoined his old firm, Goldman Sachs, as a senior advisor offering counsel on geopolitical risk, trade dynamics, and macroeconomic shifts.
John Gray, runs the world's largest manager of private capital, a total of more than $1.
3 trillion, with assets across real estate, infrastructure, life sciences, credit, insurance, private equity, renewables, and of course, data centers.

And Chandra is the leader who transformed Tata for the 21st century, building on its strength in IT services, automotive engineering, and heavy industry to enter semiconductors, advanced electronics manufacturing, electric mobility, and digital platforms, an extraordinary trio of minds to tackle this provocative conceit, the end of predictability.
Every generation thinks its moment is uniquely uncertain, right?

If you were around for the oil embargo, 1973, the Gulf War, 1991, of course, the financial crisis, 2008, what I'd like to know, and I'd like to start with you, Chandra, What is actually different about this moment in history?
First, I think we have had it very good for the last five decades.
That's what the first realization is.
But if you look at a group like ours, which is about 160 years old, we have seen two world wars, we have seen the pandemics, and we have seen high borrowing levels, many things, and we have survived.
So it's not the first time that something as hard as this is happening.
But the primary difference is all of it is happening at the same time.
The geopolitical disruption, the AI disruption, and commodity crisis, supply chain crisis, and the world has become so advanced and so connected.
We are trying to decouple it.
It has never been this coupled.
Tackling all of it at the same time is the unique thing now.
We obviously have two live wars in Russia, Ukraine, and in the Middle East with Iran and its proxies.
We obviously have an environment that has got more volatility.
We see the U.S.
With a little more tension with its allies. although I think there are enough shared values that will ultimately get through this.
I think the biggest thing, when we look back in history, when we look back 10, 20 years from now, will be the technology.
Because I think that's the thing that's going to define this era.
That we're moving from a place like we did in the U.S.

From 1870 to 1900 with the Industrial Revolution, that when you bring this superintelligence to the entire world, that it's going to profoundly change how we live, how consumers live, how businesses are impacted, and how governments oversee societies.
And to me, that's the big thing.
That's the biggest challenge.
What we are talking about is a cocktail of risks.
Geopolitics is a risk.
Technological disruption, obviously a risk.
Bad policy is a risk.
Climate events are a risk.
Market dislocations are or a risk.
Which of those risks, or perhaps a risk that I didn't mention, do you find hardest to manage?
And which worries you the most?
Rishi?
AI is often compared to the Industrial Revolution, but I think that actually undersells it.

I think of it as the Industrial Revolution combined with the Enlightenment, that period in Europe of invention and discovery of new ideas, combined with the printing press, which democratized information and knowledge around the world.
So this trifecta is going to be extraordinary.
It's going to raise the floor for humanity.
We talked about that here in India in February at the AI Summit.
However, all new technology brings with it new risks.
And what technology does is lower the barriers to entry for bad actors.
And that's what this technology does.

And I think our job as policymakers is to get ahead of that, provide safeguards, governance, and a framework so that we can not only prevent bad things from happening, but also bring along the public with us who outside of places like India or China and the Gulf are deeply distrustful of this technology.
And if we don't reassure them, we're not going to get all of its benefits.
So put aside all the geopolitics.
We'll manage that.
But John's right.
The technology is a thing that, for better or worse, we will be talking about for years to come.
Chandra, they're not the same thing, right?
The thing that you worry about the most and the thing that you find hardest to manage.
In Rishi's case, it sounds like it is the same thing.
What about for you?

Rishi is right, definitely in near term. technology both in terms of what it will do at the hands of the bad actors and also the labor restructuring that has to happen near term is going to be a big deal in medium to long term is

going to be hugely powerful it's going to make I at least think the world beautiful and highly impactful but the other thing I worry about is the war situation I think we seem to be opening wars on every front And nothing is getting closed.
So I don't know.
Somebody is going to press a button.
We should all be worried about that.
I worry about that a lot.
John? I definitely agree on both of these fronts and the technology, which I highlighted.
But since Rishi covered that, maybe I'll talk about another risk, which is the lack of fiscal sustainability. in Western governments.
Interestingly, emerging market countries in many cases have been much more responsible.
And we're now facing a bit of a reckoning.
We're seeing that in terms of what's happening in the bond market, which also the wars have contributed to the demand for capital because of AI.
But also there's.
A perception that, hey, these countries are running deficits that are well above their inherent growth rates.
And you worry, shocks come along.
You saw it with, obviously, the financial crisis, with COVID, governments now with deficits that are greater than 100% of GDP and don't seem to have a path to bend that curve.
And what happens, of course, is It leads to affordability challenges, particularly around housing.
And it means you have to make tough choices around taxes and social services.
I continue to think that technology probably is the biggest sort of existential risk.
But this is one that has been slow moving, and it's going to force very tough choices.
Just interesting, John's point there, you see these different forces coming together, right?
Because On the one hand, you've got governments who aren't able to be fiscally conservative and the kind of populist politics we're seeing across Europe and elsewhere contributing to that.

But this massive capital build-out of AI is then adding to the mix, as John knows, because the demand for capital from the technology companies is so huge that, remarkably, if you think about long-term debt, so 10-year-plus debt, next year, I think the technology companies are going to be bigger net issuers of that debt than the U.S.
Government is.
And it gives you a sense of the scale here.
But that ultimately is putting pressure on governments in Europe, contributing to some of the challenges that John mentioned.
It just speaks to the interplay between these big structural forces that we're living through.
I was just going to follow up briefly with you, John, because you can see this coming to a head right now in France.
The situation that the French are dealing with is very real.
There just simply isn't enough money.
There isn't enough money in the United States either.
Now, America has exorbitant privilege.
Perhaps that puts it in a different category.
But at what point do you begin to worry that what's going on in France is going to become a similar problem in America?
I think there's a very important difference.
I think all of these countries face this challenge.
But the growth rates in the U.S. are much higher.
And when you look at the technology.
the investment, what's happening with AI, you're seeing it lead to a lot of capital flows in.
And that higher rate of growth gives you a little more room.
Now, ultimately, the US is going to have to face tough choices.
But I think now this is more of a France, UK, continental Europe challenge, just because there you have.
Much lower rates of growth approaching, call it 1%.
But also very large deficits.
And what we've seen over time is these get addressed when there's crisis.
We saw this in Greece.
And unfortunately, that feels the way this is going.
But I would say the U.S., its great strength is both the age of its population, but also its.
Higher growth rate.
And I think people are underestimating how much growth is going to come out of the U.S. because of this investment and then productivity boom.
So that's helpful to us.
But again, we, like everybody, are going to have to find a way over time, either through much higher growth or better fiscal responsibility or a combination to get to sounder footing.
I'd like to stick.
With you for a moment because when we talk about unpredictability and we talk about risk, of course, we should be talking about how to manage, how to hedge those risks.
And the hedge for unpredictability is resilience.
But resilience is expensive, right?
It comes at a cost, efficiency.
And since we're talking.
About markets, investors really aren't very good at putting a price on resilience.
For the most part, they don't actually value resilience, just the opposite.

When you think about the need to build resilience into the investments that Blackstone makes, are you implicitly, or do you find yourself wondering whether the implicit consequence of that is that your investors are going to have to accept structurally lower returns in exchange for securing those cash flows?
There may be some of that.
I think if you went back over time, you probably just looked at where could I get the lowest cost, let's say.
Where could I source a product, set up my business to manufacture in that lowest cost location?
Optimizing for efficiency.
Optimizing for efficiency.
I think it's clear now, after you go through COVID, you go through wars, you have tariffs, you recognize if I run a manufacturing business.
I need multiple sources of input.
But I would say that we focused a lot on risks here.
It's worth pointing out that we're seeing real revenue growth globally.
So our companies in the second quarter saw 11% revenue growth.
We've seen margins consecutively go up for now two and a half, three plus years.
We've just seen steady improvement.
We see this in the public markets.
So what we're finding in our companies is even if they have some incremental costs to absorb that resilience, they're able to do it and continue to grow the businesses.
And one of the reasons you strengthen.
Markets, particularly the US markets, is because the revenue growth and the margin growth have been such that you're getting compensated even though there are more risks out there.
Chandra, how do you decide how much resilience is worth paying for?
See, I think I have a fundamentally different viewpoint.
In a highly unpredictable, volatile environment, optimizing for efficiency is definitely not the right thing.
And to think that resilience is opposite of efficiency is a wrong move.
I believe that If you design it for resilience in an unpredictable environment, actually you're optimizing for efficiency.
We had an air crash.
We had a cyber attack.
We had supply chain disruptions.
Still, as a group, we will deliver double-digit growth.
And margins are holding up.
So I think we are paying more attention.
I send the message across the group.
We have to think what is resilience for each one of our businesses.
We can't define resilience as a global thing.
Every company has to think of what is resilience.
I think if you design it for resilience, you will optimize for efficiency because that's the nature of the word.
Rishi, I made the point that markets aren't very good, or investors at least, aren't very good at valuing resilience.
But nevertheless, and we keep hearing about this, every country... wants a resilient economy.
So what happens if the market doesn't reward companies for having excess inventory, right?
Spare capacity, surplus capital, supply chain diversification.
If the market doesn't reward you for that and the genius of having it only looks brilliant in a crisis, what do you do?
Is that where government needs to step in?
Does government need to subsidize or incentivize And if so, how?
It does, but you have to be careful because politicians always like opportunities to protect local businesses.
They like opportunities to put up barriers that you protect the producers.
And this gives them an excuse to do that.
I think the instructive example here is the French.

When Pepsi, big, bad American company, tried to come and buy Danone, the important French company, the French declared that yogurt was a strategic national priority in order to block this transaction.
And that is an example of what not to do.
Having said that, it's clear, as Chandra said, the world has changed and governments need to adapt to it.
And the G7 we had when I was in office, we talked about this notion of de-risking.
Rather than decoupling.

And the National Security Advisor, Jake Sullivan, in the US actually had this concept that we put in a speech that was very good, which is this concept of a kind of small garden or small yard and a high fence.

And it's trying to figure out what are the small number of absolutely critical things that you do want to have national sovereign capability in, where you need to have a really good range of options. where you're going to prioritize to protect.
But outside of that, we should be careful to make sure that we enjoy the benefits of free markets and enterprise, which all of us realize creates growth and prosperity for our citizens.
Hard as it is sometimes to defend, Chandra and I spend an enormous amount of time working on different things together in government, and that's probably indicative of the environment that we're in.
But the other thing I'd say with that is, going back to what John said about financial market risk, I think generally this is inflationary.
It comes at a cost.
In the UK, take an example, gas storage.
John talked rightly about the supplies we've seen.
In the UK, we had our storage capacity at a rundown over time.
You have the energy shock in Europe when Russia invaded Ukraine, new energy shock now in the Middle East.
And then you realize the value of having more storage.
Ultimately, that storage comes at a cost for all the other years. that it's not used and that requires the government to step in and provide essentially some incentive to do that.
I'd like to flip the script a little bit and talk about predictability and Chandra and I have had conversations about this.

And in those conversations, Chandra, you've told me that the Tata, which to your point earlier is almost 160 years old, has learned to think in terms of generations, maybe even centuries, which is quite a thought.
Any strategy, any plan built on that kind of timeframe requires at least some certainty about the future.
What do you believe is predictable?
See, I think if you look at our own history and go back some of the decisions that were made by Jamshed G. Stein in the early 1900s, he believed that steel was fundamentally important.
Steel.
Was fundamentally important.
He felt power was fundamentally important.
He imagined a steel plant.
He imagined a hydroelectric power plant.
And he imagined R & D is important, science is important.
None of this he saw.
He didn't live to see any one of those.
But the steel plant came up in 1907, and the hydroelectric power plant came in 1911.
And they had raised money in Ohio in 1911.
So then the IASC came about.
And subsequently, there are many decisions that have been taken by people various chairmen in the group, which have all proved to be right in long term.
And sometimes things go wrong, then you course correct.
But I believe that directionally, if you design it on the belief that it is needed for India, it is needed for mankind and for enterprises, you will get it right.
Even from the time we went in, to electronics to start manufacturing, the India's exports has gone from 12 billion five years ago to 48 billion this year.
So the manufacturing sector is growing at 9%.
And advanced manufacturing is here to stay.
And if you take chips, I think if you take a vote, everyone will say chips are the future.
So whether we will get it right and meet the numbers two years or three years is not the point.
We need partnerships because we may not have all the technologies and so we need partners.
But if you design it, definitely we'll get there.
We can't be reckless in saying that I'm going to be putting a two nanometer chip.
It's just not going to work.
So we need to also see where the demand is.
But I think for me, the metric is it's important for India or it's important for businesses and people and its future.
Third, it can create jobs.
Fourth, it's financially viable.
It's not that you're going to have a very clean spreadsheet in this uncertain world, that everything is going to be certain.
But a lot of things are certain.
Direction is certain.
The need is certain.
The ability to execute is certain.
And only thing is how much you ramp up, how fast you ramp up, which technology you go to.
All this is uncertain.
John, if I look at Blackstone's track record, maybe I'll use the hockey reference, being the Canadian that I am, that you want to skate to where the puck is going, right?
Not where it is.
So where is the puck going for Blackstone next?
What is.
The next trend that you anticipate will become a big business for you.

I think we'll continue to be very long electricity because everything we're talking about around technology, the data centers, the autonomous vehicles, the robots, all of it's going to use electricity.
So this AI is going to move from the desktop to the physical world.
That'll demand more electricity.
Obviously the digital infrastructure, hugely important.

I think, unfortunately, based on the discussions here, Rishi knows better than all of us, but defense is going to be hugely important for pretty much every country in the world is going to be investing more on its own resiliency.
I think life sciences is an area that we will keep doubling down.
It'll be obviously good for India.
But this technology, which we all rightfully focus on the risks, the benefits to human health are going to be the number one thing that's going to come from it.
So there's going to be lots of innovation.
You'll still have you'll need to do a lot of trials around that.
And then I would just say geographically, because we are here, this place is It's got an incredibly bright future.

When you look at the size and age of the population, the education that's here, English speaking, lots of people with degrees in technology and engineering, a government that's pro-growth. and yet you're working off GDP per capita that's 1 30th of the United States.
Now with new infrastructure, this is.
A place when we look over the next century that I think will grow faster than any other major economy in the world.
So we want to deploy more capital here.
And Rishi, the last word on predictability goes to you.
What trends do you believe are durable enough to outlast the today's geopolitical and technological uncertainty.
It used to be said that you couldn't be a high income country without being a high energy country.
And I think John touched on that well.
I think the same will be true for intelligence and compute.
And that to me is the critical infrastructure of the next couple of decades.
And ensuring that a country has that enabling infrastructure, I think is going to be absolutely critical of the electricity powers that India's investing in it.
Countries need to do that in order to get all the benefits that John talked about, whether it's in life sciences, whether it's in productivity and elsewhere.
And we're living in the midst of this extraordinary explosion in demand for intelligence, right?
The Jivans paradox that people are familiar with from the 1860s when a new engine came along that made it all more efficient meant that the consumption of coal went up extraordinarily.
And we're seeing that today.
The demand for tokens is growing exponentially.
I think that will continue and enable all these things.
So yes, all these swirling currents are there.
But as a country or as a company, having access to that raw intelligence to power your future, I think, is the thing that you can bet on.
And alongside that, I'd say human ingenuity, right?
No matter what comes our way, we are always able to find solutions, right?

So I would always bet on human ingenuity, whether it's in countries like India or elsewhere, the people who are innovating, the entrepreneurs who are creating new things, supporting them and allowing their ideas to flourish and grow.
That's ultimately how you develop not just security, but also prosperity and health to your society.
An appropriate note of optimism on which to end our conversation.
Rishi Sunak, John Gray, Chandra, distinguished guests, please join me in thanking them.
Thank you, Rishi.
Thanks for listening to Trumponomics from Bloomberg.
It was hosted by me, Stephanie Flanders, and I was joined here in Delhi by Bloomberg's chief economist, Tom Orlick.

segments.text: Now, I was thinking back, Elon Musk, I seem to remember, accused Christopher Nolan of trashing Homer's grave.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That film.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: was a woke.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Cry of pain for the end of the rule-based global order, which obviously Elon Musk didn't like. Ezra Klein, the columnist for the New York Times, thought that was precisely why it was, in his words, the political movie of the decade. Everybody found something in that film. Tom, you saw lessons for economic policy in it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: I'm sure classics scholars would tell me that this is off-base, Stephanie, but it seems to me that one of the themes that comes through in The Odyssey is this idea of a world where the rules of hospitality have broken down. You see it in Polyphemus the Cyclops, a host who eats his guests. You see it in Penelope's suitors, guests in Odysseus's house, eating his food, drinking his wine, trying to steal his wife.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: I thought this idea of the Odyssey and a world where the rules of hospitality have broken down will be a kind of neat framing for a presentation to the audience.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: So what are some of the consequences from an economic standpoint of this world where the rules of hospitality are broken down?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: So I think one of the places where we're seeing this dynamic play out is in the US bond market. If we think about the cost of borrowing for the US Treasury, back in 1980, that was around 15%. Over many decades, the cost of borrowing for the US Treasury fell and fell until by 2020, it was close to zero. Now, in the last few years, that trajectory has changed, and the cost of borrowing for the US isn't falling anymore.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: It's rising. The 10-year rate is now north of 5%. And I think that's a reflection of some of these big dynamics that we're seeing. A world where war is more likely, and so companies have to borrow more to pay for defense. A world where there's been rupture between the US and China, the US and Russia, the US and the petrostates. So these countries, which in the past were willing to put their savings to work in the US treasury market, are now not doing that anymore.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: And a world where geopolitical shocks like the Iran war are pushing inflation higher. And of course, bond investors need to be compensated for higher inflation. So in this world where the rules of hospitality have broken down, the US Treasury has to pay more to borrow. And of course, when the US Treasury has to pay more to borrow, everybody has to pay more to borrow. A fact which is pretty consequential for our hosts here in India, hoping to attract more FDI to finance the build-out of their infrastructure and their manufacturing base.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: One of the other themes that came through, which obviously has been much discussed in this conference, is AI is actually something that might surprise some people, that we have seen with the build-out of AI, in many ways, a kind of reassertion of global supply chains, at least in a certain part of the economy, and reanimation of globalisation and trade. And with that... the return of very large global imbalances.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: So despite Donald Trump's best efforts, China exporting more than it ever has. We actually had new record trade surplus numbers coming out of China this week. And the US, despite Donald Trump's efforts, importing, we reckon, $500 billion more a year than in 2016. That's allowing for inflation, not all from China, but it has in many ways become more dependent on the rest of the world as a result of, in part, AI and other things about the way the world has gone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: But as you pointed out, the flip side of that is big trade surplus and surplus revenues for China, Korea, Taiwan are We've seen those before. They used to be invested via central banks into US treasuries often. What's different this time?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's strange.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: President Trump imposed these sweeping tariffs to try and reduce the US trade deficit, reduce the Chinese trade surplus. In fact, what we've seen in the last couple of years is actually those surpluses and deficits have exploded higher, right? We've now got surpluses in China, Taiwan, Korea, and deficits in the US that are bigger in dollar terms than they were back in the early 2000s before the global financial crisis.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: But as you note, Stephanie, there's also a different dynamic at work. In the early 2000s, let's take China as an example, the trade surplus meant a huge pileup of dollar savings in the economy. Those dollar savings were managed by the People's Bank of China Central Bank, a very conservative buy and hold investor. And the PBOC put those dollars into the US Treasury market, the most stable, safest asset in the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: This time around, the savings piling up in East Asian countries, they're not being managed by central banks. They're being managed by private investors, much more nimble, much more focused on returns, And when we look at the data, what we see is they're not going into the treasury market anymore. That's one of the reasons the treasury is having to pay more to borrow. They're going into stocks. They're going into corporate bonds.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: The pretty clear signal is that they're going into the AI revolution, right? So you've got this circular flow of funds where the US is importing a huge amount of chips to build out its data centers and And the countries making those chips are taking the dollars the US is paying them and turning around and investing them back in the US AI companies. Now, if you're an AI optimist, and there's lots of reasons to be an AI optimist, that's all good, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: AI is going to make us better off. This is accelerating the AI revolution, which is going to make us all better off. But if you're an AI pessimist, And you think the profits from AI might turn up a day late and a dollar short. And there's going to be a moment where there's a big adjustment in the markets, a crash. This dynamic means the pain from that crash is going to be spread out around the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: It does certainly sound like a risky combination. What was striking to me was A slightly different view from that panel I mentioned at the start, although they, at least one of them, was pretty focused on the risks lurking in government debt and government balance sheet. So let's hear from that now. And I'm actually going to let my colleague, Eric Schatzker, the editorial director of NEF, who presided over the panel, do the introduction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Distinguished guests, I'd like to say a few things about our panelists to explain why we've invited them to join me here on stage this morning. Rishi Sunak, as you know, is a sitting member of parliament in the UK and, of course, the country's former prime minister. He has become a strategic voice in Silicon Valley as an advisor and also as a visiting fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: He has also rejoined his old firm, Goldman Sachs, as a senior advisor offering counsel on geopolitical risk, trade dynamics, and macroeconomic shifts. John Gray, runs the world's largest manager of private capital, a total of more than $1. 3 trillion, with assets across real estate, infrastructure, life sciences, credit, insurance, private equity, renewables, and of course, data centers. And Chandra is the leader who transformed Tata for the 21st century, building on its strength in IT services, automotive engineering, and heavy industry to enter semiconductors, advanced electronics manufacturing, electric mobility, and digital platforms, an extraordinary trio of minds to tackle this provocative conceit, the end of predictability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Every generation thinks its moment is uniquely uncertain, right? If you were around for the oil embargo, 1973, the Gulf War, 1991, of course, the financial crisis, 2008, what I'd like to know, and I'd like to start with you, Chandra, What is actually different about this moment in history?

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: First, I think we have had it very good for the last five decades. That's what the first realization is. But if you look at a group like ours, which is about 160 years old, we have seen two world wars, we have seen the pandemics, and we have seen high borrowing levels, many things, and we have survived. So it's not the first time that something as hard as this is happening.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: But the primary difference is all of it is happening at the same time. The geopolitical disruption, the AI disruption, and commodity crisis, supply chain crisis, and the world has become so advanced and so connected. We are trying to decouple it. It has never been this coupled.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Tackling all of it at the same time is the unique thing now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: We obviously have two live wars in Russia, Ukraine, and in the Middle East with Iran and its proxies. We obviously have an environment that has got more volatility.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We see the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: With a little more tension with its allies. although I think there are enough shared values that will ultimately get through this. I think the biggest thing, when we look back in history, when we look back 10, 20 years from now, will be the technology. Because I think that's the thing that's going to define this era.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That we're moving from a place like we did in the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: From 1870 to 1900 with the Industrial Revolution, that when you bring this superintelligence to the entire world, that it's going to profoundly change how we live, how consumers live, how businesses are impacted, and how governments oversee societies. And to me, that's the big thing. That's the biggest challenge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: What we are talking about is a cocktail of risks. Geopolitics is a risk. Technological disruption, obviously a risk. Bad policy is a risk. Climate events are a risk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Market dislocations are or a risk.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Which of those risks, or perhaps a risk that I didn't mention, do you find hardest to manage? And which worries you the most?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Rishi?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: AI is often compared to the Industrial Revolution, but I think that actually undersells it. I think of it as the Industrial Revolution combined with the Enlightenment, that period in Europe of invention and discovery of new ideas, combined with the printing press, which democratized information and knowledge around the world. So this trifecta is going to be extraordinary. It's going to raise the floor for humanity. We talked about that here in India in February at the AI Summit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: However, all new technology brings with it new risks. And what technology does is lower the barriers to entry for bad actors. And that's what this technology does. And I think our job as policymakers is to get ahead of that, provide safeguards, governance, and a framework so that we can not only prevent bad things from happening, but also bring along the public with us who outside of places like India or China and the Gulf are deeply distrustful of this technology.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And if we don't reassure them, we're not going to get all of its benefits. So put aside all the geopolitics. We'll manage that. But John's right. The technology is a thing that, for better or worse, we will be talking about for years to come.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Chandra, they're not the same thing, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: The thing that you worry about the most and the thing that you find hardest to manage. In Rishi's case, it sounds like it is the same thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What about for you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Rishi is right, definitely in near term. technology both in terms of what it will do at the hands of the bad actors and also the labor restructuring that has to happen near term is going to be a big deal in medium to long term is going to be hugely powerful it's going to make I at least think the world beautiful and highly impactful but the other thing I worry about is the war situation I think we seem to be opening wars on every front And nothing is getting closed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: So I don't know. Somebody is going to press a button.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We should all be worried about that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: I worry about that a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: John? I definitely agree on both of these fronts and the technology, which I highlighted. But since Rishi covered that, maybe I'll talk about another risk, which is the lack of fiscal sustainability. in Western governments. Interestingly, emerging market countries in many cases have been much more responsible. And we're now facing a bit of a reckoning. We're seeing that in terms of what's happening in the bond market, which also the wars have contributed to the demand for capital because of AI.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But also there's.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: A perception that, hey, these countries are running deficits that are well above their inherent growth rates. And you worry, shocks come along. You saw it with, obviously, the financial crisis, with COVID, governments now with deficits that are greater than 100% of GDP and don't seem to have a path to bend that curve. And what happens, of course, is It leads to affordability challenges, particularly around housing. And it means you have to make tough choices around taxes and social services.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I continue to think that technology probably is the biggest sort of existential risk. But this is one that has been slow moving, and it's going to force very tough choices.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Just interesting, John's point there, you see these different forces coming together, right? Because On the one hand, you've got governments who aren't able to be fiscally conservative and the kind of populist politics we're seeing across Europe and elsewhere contributing to that. But this massive capital build-out of AI is then adding to the mix, as John knows, because the demand for capital from the technology companies is so huge that, remarkably, if you think about long-term debt, so 10-year-plus debt, next year, I think the technology companies are going to be bigger net issuers of that debt than the U.S.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Government is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And it gives you a sense of the scale here. But that ultimately is putting pressure on governments in Europe, contributing to some of the challenges that John mentioned. It just speaks to the interplay between these big structural forces that we're living through.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: I was just going to follow up briefly with you, John, because you can see this coming to a head right now in France. The situation that the French are dealing with is very real. There just simply isn't enough money. There isn't enough money in the United States either. Now, America has exorbitant privilege. Perhaps that puts it in a different category. But at what point do you begin to worry that what's going on in France is going to become a similar problem in America?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I think there's a very important difference. I think all of these countries face this challenge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But the growth rates in the U.S. are much higher. And when you look at the technology.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: the investment, what's happening with AI, you're seeing it lead to a lot of capital flows in. And that higher rate of growth gives you a little more room. Now, ultimately, the US is going to have to face tough choices. But I think now this is more of a France, UK, continental Europe challenge, just because there you have.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Much lower rates of growth approaching, call it 1%.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But also very large deficits.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And what we've seen over time is these get addressed when there's crisis. We saw this in Greece. And unfortunately, that feels the way this is going. But I would say the U.S., its great strength is both the age of its population, but also its.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Higher growth rate.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And I think people are underestimating how much growth is going to come out of the U.S. because of this investment and then productivity boom. So that's helpful to us. But again, we, like everybody, are going to have to find a way over time, either through much higher growth or better fiscal responsibility or a combination to get to sounder footing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'd like to stick.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: With you for a moment because when we talk about unpredictability and we talk about risk, of course, we should be talking about how to manage, how to hedge those risks. And the hedge for unpredictability is resilience. But resilience is expensive, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It comes at a cost, efficiency. And since we're talking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: About markets, investors really aren't very good at putting a price on resilience. For the most part, they don't actually value resilience, just the opposite. When you think about the need to build resilience into the investments that Blackstone makes, are you implicitly, or do you find yourself wondering whether the implicit consequence of that is that your investors are going to have to accept structurally lower returns in exchange for securing those cash flows?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There may be some of that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I think if you went back over time, you probably just looked at where could I get the lowest cost, let's say. Where could I source a product, set up my business to manufacture in that lowest cost location?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Optimizing for efficiency. Optimizing for efficiency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I think it's clear now, after you go through COVID, you go through wars, you have tariffs, you recognize if I run a manufacturing business.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I need multiple sources of input.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: But I would say that we focused a lot on risks here. It's worth pointing out that we're seeing real revenue growth globally. So our companies in the second quarter saw 11% revenue growth. We've seen margins consecutively go up for now two and a half, three plus years.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We've just seen steady improvement. We see this in the public markets.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: So what we're finding in our companies is even if they have some incremental costs to absorb that resilience, they're able to do it and continue to grow the businesses.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And one of the reasons you strengthen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Markets, particularly the US markets, is because the revenue growth and the margin growth have been such that you're getting compensated even though there are more risks out there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Chandra, how do you decide how much resilience is worth paying for?

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: See, I think I have a fundamentally different viewpoint. In a highly unpredictable, volatile environment, optimizing for efficiency is definitely not the right thing. And to think that resilience is opposite of efficiency is a wrong move. I believe that If you design it for resilience in an unpredictable environment, actually you're optimizing for efficiency. We had an air crash. We had a cyber attack. We had supply chain disruptions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Still, as a group, we will deliver double-digit growth. And margins are holding up. So I think we are paying more attention. I send the message across the group. We have to think what is resilience for each one of our businesses. We can't define resilience as a global thing. Every company has to think of what is resilience. I think if you design it for resilience, you will optimize for efficiency because that's the nature of the word.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Rishi, I made the point that markets aren't very good, or investors at least, aren't very good at valuing resilience. But nevertheless, and we keep hearing about this, every country... wants a resilient economy. So what happens if the market doesn't reward companies for having excess inventory, right? Spare capacity, surplus capital, supply chain diversification. If the market doesn't reward you for that and the genius of having it only looks brilliant in a crisis, what do you do?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is that where government needs to step in?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Does government need to subsidize or incentivize And if so, how?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It does, but you have to be careful because politicians always like opportunities to protect local businesses. They like opportunities to put up barriers that you protect the producers. And this gives them an excuse to do that. I think the instructive example here is the French. When Pepsi, big, bad American company, tried to come and buy Danone, the important French company, the French declared that yogurt was a strategic national priority in order to block this transaction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And that is an example of what not to do. Having said that, it's clear, as Chandra said, the world has changed and governments need to adapt to it. And the G7 we had when I was in office, we talked about this notion of de-risking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Rather than decoupling.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the National Security Advisor, Jake Sullivan, in the US actually had this concept that we put in a speech that was very good, which is this concept of a kind of small garden or small yard and a high fence. And it's trying to figure out what are the small number of absolutely critical things that you do want to have national sovereign capability in, where you need to have a really good range of options. where you're going to prioritize to protect.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: But outside of that, we should be careful to make sure that we enjoy the benefits of free markets and enterprise, which all of us realize creates growth and prosperity for our citizens. Hard as it is sometimes to defend, Chandra and I spend an enormous amount of time working on different things together in government, and that's probably indicative of the environment that we're in. But the other thing I'd say with that is, going back to what John said about financial market risk, I think generally this is inflationary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It comes at a cost. In the UK, take an example, gas storage. John talked rightly about the supplies we've seen. In the UK, we had our storage capacity at a rundown over time. You have the energy shock in Europe when Russia invaded Ukraine, new energy shock now in the Middle East. And then you realize the value of having more storage. Ultimately, that storage comes at a cost for all the other years. that it's not used and that requires the government to step in and provide essentially some incentive to do that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: I'd like to flip the script a little bit and talk about predictability and Chandra and I have had conversations about this. And in those conversations, Chandra, you've told me that the Tata, which to your point earlier is almost 160 years old, has learned to think in terms of generations, maybe even centuries, which is quite a thought. Any strategy, any plan built on that kind of timeframe requires at least some certainty about the future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: What do you believe is predictable?

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: See, I think if you look at our own history and go back some of the decisions that were made by Jamshed G. Stein in the early 1900s, he believed that steel was fundamentally important.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Steel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Was fundamentally important. He felt power was fundamentally important. He imagined a steel plant. He imagined a hydroelectric power plant. And he imagined R & D is important, science is important. None of this he saw. He didn't live to see any one of those. But the steel plant came up in 1907, and the hydroelectric power plant came in 1911. And they had raised money in Ohio in 1911.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: So then the IASC came about. And subsequently, there are many decisions that have been taken by people various chairmen in the group, which have all proved to be right in long term. And sometimes things go wrong, then you course correct. But I believe that directionally, if you design it on the belief that it is needed for India, it is needed for mankind and for enterprises, you will get it right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Even from the time we went in, to electronics to start manufacturing, the India's exports has gone from 12 billion five years ago to 48 billion this year. So the manufacturing sector is growing at 9%. And advanced manufacturing is here to stay. And if you take chips, I think if you take a vote, everyone will say chips are the future. So whether we will get it right and meet the numbers two years or three years is not the point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: We need partnerships because we may not have all the technologies and so we need partners. But if you design it, definitely we'll get there. We can't be reckless in saying that I'm going to be putting a two nanometer chip. It's just not going to work. So we need to also see where the demand is. But I think for me, the metric is it's important for India or it's important for businesses and people and its future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Third, it can create jobs. Fourth, it's financially viable. It's not that you're going to have a very clean spreadsheet in this uncertain world, that everything is going to be certain. But a lot of things are certain. Direction is certain. The need is certain. The ability to execute is certain. And only thing is how much you ramp up, how fast you ramp up, which technology you go to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: All this is uncertain.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: John, if I look at Blackstone's track record, maybe I'll use the hockey reference, being the Canadian that I am, that you want to skate to where the puck is going, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Not where it is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: So where is the puck going for Blackstone next?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: The next trend that you anticipate will become a big business for you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I think we'll continue to be very long electricity because everything we're talking about around technology, the data centers, the autonomous vehicles, the robots, all of it's going to use electricity. So this AI is going to move from the desktop to the physical world. That'll demand more electricity. Obviously the digital infrastructure, hugely important. I think, unfortunately, based on the discussions here, Rishi knows better than all of us, but defense is going to be hugely important for pretty much every country in the world is going to be investing more on its own resiliency.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I think life sciences is an area that we will keep doubling down. It'll be obviously good for India. But this technology, which we all rightfully focus on the risks, the benefits to human health are going to be the number one thing that's going to come from it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So there's going to be lots of innovation. You'll still have you'll need to do a lot of trials around that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And then I would just say geographically, because we are here, this place is It's got an incredibly bright future. When you look at the size and age of the population, the education that's here, English speaking, lots of people with degrees in technology and engineering, a government that's pro-growth. and yet you're working off GDP per capita that's 1 30th of the United States.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Now with new infrastructure, this is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: A place when we look over the next century that I think will grow faster than any other major economy in the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So we want to deploy more capital here.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: And Rishi, the last word on predictability goes to you. What trends do you believe are durable enough to outlast the today's geopolitical and technological uncertainty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It used to be said that you couldn't be a high income country without being a high energy country. And I think John touched on that well. I think the same will be true for intelligence and compute. And that to me is the critical infrastructure of the next couple of decades. And ensuring that a country has that enabling infrastructure, I think is going to be absolutely critical of the electricity powers that India's investing in it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Countries need to do that in order to get all the benefits that John talked about, whether it's in life sciences, whether it's in productivity and elsewhere. And we're living in the midst of this extraordinary explosion in demand for intelligence, right? The Jivans paradox that people are familiar with from the 1860s when a new engine came along that made it all more efficient meant that the consumption of coal went up extraordinarily.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And we're seeing that today. The demand for tokens is growing exponentially. I think that will continue and enable all these things. So yes, all these swirling currents are there. But as a country or as a company, having access to that raw intelligence to power your future, I think, is the thing that you can bet on. And alongside that, I'd say human ingenuity, right? No matter what comes our way, we are always able to find solutions, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So I would always bet on human ingenuity, whether it's in countries like India or elsewhere, the people who are innovating, the entrepreneurs who are creating new things, supporting them and allowing their ideas to flourish and grow. That's ultimately how you develop not just security, but also prosperity and health to your society.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: An appropriate note of optimism on which to end our conversation. Rishi Sunak, John Gray, Chandra, distinguished guests, please join me in thanking them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Thank you, Rishi.

segments.text: Thanks for listening to Trumponomics from Bloomberg. It was hosted by me, Stephanie Flanders, and I was joined here in Delhi by Bloomberg's chief economist, Tom Orlick. study.one_liner_ko: 뉴델리 New Economy Forum에서 Tom Orlik이 미 국채 금리 상승과 AI 자금 순환의 위험을 짚고, Sunak·Gray·Chandrasekaran이 불확실성 시대의 위험, 회복탄력성, 그래도 베팅할 만한 장기 트렌드를 논했다.
summary_ko: Bloomberg 수석이코노미스트 Tom Orlik은 영화 '오디세이'의 '환대의 규칙이 무너진 세계'를 틀로 삼았다. 전쟁, 미중·미러 단절, 이란전쟁발 인플레이션 때문에 미 국채 10년물 금리가 5%를 넘었고, 그 여파로 모든 차입 비용이 오른다고 설명한다.
트럼프 관세에도 미국의 무역적자와 중국·대만·한국의 흑자는 2000년대 초보다 더 커졌다. 달라진 점은 흑자 자금을 보수적인 중앙은행이 아니라 민간 투자자가 굴리고, 이 돈이 국채가 아니라 미국 AI 기업으로 되돌아가는 순환 구조라는 것이다. AI가 기대에 못 미치면 폭락의 고통이 전 세계로 퍼진다.
패널에서 Chandrasekaran은 이번 위기의 차이를 지정학, AI, 원자재, 공급망 위기가 동시에 온다는 점에서 찾았다. Jon Gray와 Rishi Sunak은 AI를 산업혁명에 계몽주의가 더해진 변화로 보면서, 악의적 행위자와 대중의 불신을 관리할 거버넌스가 필요하다고 했다.
Gray는 서방 정부의 재정 지속가능성을 가장 큰 위험 중 하나로 꼽았다. Sunak은 내년에 기술기업이 미 정부보다 장기채를 더 많이 발행할 수 있다며, AI의 자본 수요가 정부를 압박한다고 지적했다. 미국은 성장률이 높아 여유가 있지만 프랑스·영국·유럽대륙은 위기가 와야 해결될 가능성이 크다는 게 Gray의 진단이다.
회복탄력성을 두고 Gray는 비용이 들지만 기업들이 감당하고 있다고 했고, Chandra는 불확실한 환경에서는 회복탄력성 중심 설계가 곧 효율 최적화라고 반박했다. Sunak은 보호주의로 흐르지 않도록 '작은 마당, 높은 울타리'식으로 핵심 분야만 정부가 지원하라고 했다.
마지막으로 베팅할 장기 트렌드는 전력, 디지털 인프라, 국방, 생명과학, 인도의 성장, 그리고 지능·컴퓨트에 대한 접근과 인간의 창의성이다. Sunak은 제번스 역설을 들어 토큰 수요가 기하급수적으로 늘 것이라고 했다.
study.summary_en: So this episode was recorded live at Bloomberg's New Economy Forum in New Delhi. Tom Orlik explained that US borrowing costs are now north of 5% because of war, geopolitical rupture and inflation, and that surplus savings in Asia are flowing into US AI companies instead of Treasuries. That makes a potential AI crash a global problem. Then a panel with Rishi Sunak, Jon Gray and Chandra debated risk. Their biggest worries were AI misuse, wars, and Western fiscal sustainability. They disagreed a bit on resilience versus efficiency, but all of them said they'd bet on electricity, compute, life sciences, India's growth, and human ingenuity.

expressions.expression: a day late and a dollar short
expressions.quote: turn up a day late and a dollar short
expressions.meaning_ko: 너무 늦고 모자라서 소용없는 (뒤늦은 데다 부족한)
expressions.nuance_ko: 타이밍도 놓치고 규모도 부족한 결과를 비꼬며 말할 때 쓴다. 구어체 관용구이고 약간 냉소적이라, 회의에서는 비판이나 회의론을 표현할 때 적당하다.
examples: Their response to the outage was a day late and a dollar short.
If we launch after the competitor, we'll be a day late and a dollar short.
The city's new bus lanes feel a day late and a dollar short.

similar.example: The apology was too little, too late.
If we wait any longer, we'll miss the boat on this deal.

expressions.quote: the flip side of that is big trade surplus
expressions.nuance_ko: 앞서 말한 것의 짝이 되는 반대 측면을 소개할 때 쓰는 담론표지. 'on the other hand'보다 구어적이고, 인과적으로 맞물린 이면을 말할 때 자연스럽다.
examples: Remote work saves commuting time, but the flip side of that is you never really switch off.
Cheap flights are great; the flip side of that is overcrowded old towns.
We got a big raise, and the flip side of that is much higher expectations.

similar.example: The downside is that it takes forever to get a table.
Conversely, a weaker currency helps exporters.

expressions.quote: we're seeing this dynamic play out is in the US bond market
expressions.nuance_ko: 'see something play out'은 어떤 역학이나 시나리오가 실제로 나타나는 모습을 말할 때 쓴다. 'happen'보다 과정이 진행되는 느낌이 강하고, 분석 톤의 대화에 잘 맞는다.
examples: Let's see how the negotiations play out before we commit.
You can watch the same pattern play out in every election.
I'm curious how this plays out over the next six months.

similar.example: The story is still unfolding.
Let's see how it shakes out.

expressions.quote: The 10-year rate is now north of 5%.
expressions.nuance_ko: 숫자 앞에서 'more than'의 구어체 대용으로 쓰며 기자·금융인이 자주 쓴다. 정확한 수치보다 '꽤 넘는다'는 뉘앙스다. 반대는 'south of'.
examples: Rent in that neighborhood is north of three thousand a month.
We had north of fifty people at the meetup.
Flights to Tokyo are running north of a thousand dollars right now.

similar.example: The bill came to in excess of ten thousand dollars.
It cost well over budget.

expressions.quote: I'd like to flip the script a little bit and talk about predictability
expressions.meaning_ko: 기존 흐름·역할을 뒤집다, 관점을 확 바꾸다
expressions.nuance_ko: 진행자가 대화의 방향을 바꿀 때나 예상과 정반대의 전개를 만들 때 쓴다. 비격식이지만 패널과 인터뷰에서도 자연스럽다.
examples: Instead of me pitching you, let me flip the script and ask what you need.
The startup flipped the script on the big incumbents.
Let's flip the script: what if the customer set the price?

similar.example: Now the tables have turned, and they need us.
We changed tack halfway through the meeting.

expressions.expression: skate to where the puck is going
expressions.quote: you want to skate to where the puck is going, right?
expressions.meaning_ko: 현재가 아니라 앞으로 흐름이 향할 곳을 선점하다
expressions.nuance_ko: 하키 비유로, 지금 상황이 아니라 미래의 위치를 예측하고 움직이라는 전략 조언이다. 보통 'not where it is'와 붙여 쓰고 비즈니스·투자 대화에서 인기 있다.
examples: In hiring, you have to skate to where the puck is going, not where it is.
Smart companies skate to where the puck is going on regulation.
I'm choosing a degree based on where the puck is going, not where it is today.

similar.example: We want to stay ahead of the curve on privacy rules.
We should future-proof the contract.

expressions.quote: an area that we will keep doubling down
expressions.meaning_ko: (기존 선택에) 더 크게 걸다, 투자를 더 강화하다
expressions.nuance_ko: 이미 선택한 방향에 힘을 더 싣는다는 뜻. 'double down on'을 쓰는데, 실패해도 고집을 부린다는 부정적 느낌으로도 쓰이므로 문맥에 주의한다.
examples: After the good reviews, they doubled down on the new menu.
He just doubled down on his claim instead of admitting the mistake.
We're doubling down on customer support this quarter.

similar.example: We should lean into what makes us different.
They went all in on video.

expressions.quote: you can see this coming to a head right now in France
expressions.nuance_ko: 오래 쌓인 갈등이나 문제가 더는 무시할 수 없는 지점에 도달했을 때 쓴다. 보통 부정적 상황에 쓰며 'bring something to a head'로도 쓴다.
examples: The tension between the two teams finally came to a head last week.
The housing problem is coming to a head in many big cities.
Their disagreement came to a head during the budget meeting.

similar.example: Things reached a boiling point after the layoffs.
Customers hit a breaking point with the delays.

expressions.quote: don't seem to have a path to bend that curve
expressions.nuance_ko: 부채, 비용, 감염자 수처럼 오르는 곡선의 방향을 바꿀 때 쓴다. 팬데믹 때 널리 퍼졌고 정책·경영 토론에서 자주 쓴다.
examples: We need to bend the curve on healthcare costs.
It's hard to bend the curve on emissions without industry buy-in.
The new policy has barely bent the curve on traffic.

similar.example: The new coach turned the tide for the team.
We have to reverse the trend in churn.

expressions.quote: I think that actually undersells it.
expressions.meaning_ko: 실제보다 과소평가하게 만들다, 제 가치를 못 담다
expressions.nuance_ko: 비교나 표현이 대상의 중요성을 충분히 전달하지 못한다고 반박할 때 쓰는 세련된 표현이다. 'X undersells it'은 'X로는 부족하다'는 뜻이고, 'undersell oneself'는 자신을 낮추는 것.
examples: Calling it a 'nice little café' really undersells it.
Don't undersell yourself in the interview.
'Challenging' undersells how bad the situation is.

similar.example: Words can't do justice to the view.
That figure understates the problem.

expressions.quote: Having said that, it's clear, as Chandra said, the world has changed
expressions.meaning_ko: 그렇긴 하지만 (앞 주장에 단서를 달 때)
expressions.nuance_ko: 앞서 한 주장을 일부 인정하면서 균형 잡힌 반론이나 단서를 붙일 때 쓴다. 'however'보다 말하기에서 자연스럽고 신중한 인상을 준다.
examples: It's a great offer. Having said that, I'd want to see the contract first.
I love the city. Having said that, I couldn't live there long-term.
The numbers look good; having said that, they rely on one big client.

similar.example: That said, we should still double-check.
Even so, I'm not convinced.

expressions.quote: sometimes things go wrong, then you course correct.
expressions.nuance_ko: 큰 방향은 유지하면서 잘못된 부분을 조정한다는 점잖은 표현이다. 'admit failure'보다 부담이 적어 경영·정치 담화에서 즐겨 쓴다.
examples: If the pilot goes badly, we'll course correct quickly.
She noticed the drift early and course corrected.
The company had to course correct after the product backlash.

similar.example: We adjusted course after the first quarter.
We need to recalibrate our targets.

expressions.quote: What we are talking about is a cocktail of risks.
expressions.nuance_ko: 'a cocktail of X'는 서로 다른 요소가 섞여 상승효과를 낼 때 쓴다. 보통 위험, 약물, 감정 등 부정적 맥락과 어울리고 'toxic cocktail'로도 쓴다.
examples: High prices, low wages and rising rents make a toxic cocktail for young people.
The trip was a cocktail of excitement and exhaustion.
A cocktail of factors led to the delay.

similar.example: It was a perfect storm of bad timing and bad luck.
It's a mix of both.

vocab.example: After years of overspending, the company faced a reckoning.
Small teams are more nimble than big corporations.
The conceit of the film is that time runs backwards.
The strike caused major dislocation across the transport network.
The argument led to a rupture between the two founders.
Good weather, great food and cheap flights: a holiday trifecta.
There's a pileup of unanswered emails on my desk.
With a bit of ingenuity, we fixed it with tape and a paperclip.

warmup.q: When you hear 'uncertain times,' what's the first risk that comes to your mind, and why?
warmup.hint_ko: 지정학, 기술, 경제 중 하나를 골라 개인적 경험이나 뉴스와 연결해 말하기.

warmup.q: Do you tend to be an AI optimist or an AI pessimist in your daily work?
warmup.hint_ko: 업무에서 쓰는 사례, 기대와 우려를 균형 있게 언급.

opinion.q: Tom Orlik says that if the AI boom turns out to be a day late and a dollar short, the pain would be global. How worried should we be?
opinion.hint_ko: AI 투자 과열 징후, 자금 순환 구조, 비관·낙관 시나리오를 비교. 개인 의견을 한 문장으로 먼저 제시.

opinion.q: Chandra says designing for resilience actually optimizes for efficiency. Do you buy that?
opinion.hint_ko: 단기 비용 대 장기 안정성, 자신의 조직이나 산업 사례를 들어 설명.

opinion.q: Which trend would you bet on for the next twenty years, and why?
opinion.hint_ko: 전력, 컴퓨트, 생명과학, 인구 구조 등에서 하나를 골라 근거 2개 제시.

debate.q: Should governments pay companies to hold spare capacity, inventory and diversified supply chains?
debate.for: 시장은 회복탄력성을 가격에 반영하지 못하므로 위기 때 사회 전체가 큰 비용을 치른다. 가스 저장처럼 핵심 분야에는 정부 인센티브가 필요하다.
debate.against: 보호주의와 특정 산업 로비의 구실이 되어 비용과 인플레이션을 키운다. 프랑스의 요거트 사례처럼 '전략 산업' 범위가 끝없이 넓어질 수 있다.

debate.q: Is the US growth advantage enough to avoid a European-style fiscal reckoning?
debate.for: 높은 성장률, 젊은 인구, AI 투자와 생산성 붐이 부채 부담에 여유를 준다.
debate.against: 100%가 넘는 GDP 대비 부채와 적자는 성장만으로 해결하기 어렵고, 금리가 오르면 이자 부담이 빠르게 커진다.

roleplay.scenario: You are on a panel at an industry conference discussing how your company should handle a cocktail of risks (supply chain, AI disruption, geopolitics). The moderator pushes you on resilience versus efficiency.
roleplay.partner_role: Skeptical moderator who challenges your assumptions
goals: Use at least three target expressions (e.g., 'flip side', 'having said that', 'course correct', 'double down').
Present a clear position on resilience versus efficiency with one concrete example.
Acknowledge a counterargument and respond to it diplomatically.

useful_phrases.phrase: The flip side of that is…
I'd like to flip the script a little bit.

useful_phrases.ko: 그건 실제보다 너무 낮춰 말한 것이다

useful_phrases.phrase: It's the interplay between these forces.
That's the thing you can bet on.

shadowing.reason_ko: 낙관론과 비관론을 대비시키는 구조와 'a day late and a dollar short' 관용구를 한 번에 연습할 수 있다.
비유로 문제를 재정의하고('undersells it'), 위험과 정책 대응으로 논리를 이어가는 매끄러운 패널 발언의 전형이다.
'I have a fundamentally different viewpoint'로 정중하게 반박하고 논리를 뒤집는 설득형 화법을 익힐 수 있다.

difficulty.note_ko: 거시경제·금융 용어(국채 금리, 재정 적자, 무역수지)와 패널 특유의 빠른 발화가 많지만 문장 구조는 명료하다. 관용구와 담론표지가 풍부해 패널·회의용 표현 학습에 좋다. 자동 전사 때문에 일부 화자 라벨과 고유명사 표기가 어긋난다.

translations_sent.3-3: 뉴스. 10년, 20년 뒤에 역사를 돌아본다면 가장 큰 건 기술이 될 거라고 생각합니다.
translations_sent.4-4: 이 시대를 규정할 게 바로 기술이라고 보거든요.
translations_sent.5-5: 미국이 1870년부터 1900년까지 산업혁명을 겪었던 것처럼, 지금 우리는 초지능을 전 세계에 가져오는 단계로 가고 있고, 그렇게 되면 우리가 사는 방식, 소비자의 삶, 기업이 받는 영향, 그리고 정부가 사회를 감독하는 방식까지 근본적으로 바뀔 겁니다.
translations_sent.7-7: 저는 블룸버그 정부·경제 부문 총괄 스테파니 플랜더스입니다. 여기는 도널드 트럼프의 경제 세계 전반을 다루는 팟캐스트, 트럼포노믹스입니다.
translations_sent.8-8: 이번 주에 저는 인도에 와 있는데요, 블룸버그가 뉴델리에서 처음으로 연례 뉴 이코노미 포럼을 열고 있습니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 재계와 금융계의 저명인사들이 대거 참석했고, 세계 각국의 정부 장관들도 많이 와 있습니다.
translations_sent.10-10: 제가 센 것만 최소 열두 명은 됩니다.
translations_sent.11-11: 지금은 수요일, 행사 이틀째에 녹음하고 있는데요, 어제 열린 아주 성대한 개막 세션에서는 나렌드라 모디 총리가 열정적인 연설을 했습니다.
translations_sent.12-12: 솔직히 그 연설은 녹음으로 들으면 현장 분위기가 잘 안 전해질 것 같아서 들려드리지는 않겠습니다.
